To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
recombinant TNF binding protein‐1 (rTBP1) significantly increases the in vitro clonogenic growth in hematopoietic cells from HIV‐infected individuals.
the p55 soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor (TBP‐1), which is a TNF‐binding molecule, was found to enhance the growth of hematopoetic progenitor cells from AIDS patients.

recombinant tumor necrosis factor binding protein‐1 (rTBP) increased colony‐forming unit (CFU) formation of myelomonocytic colony forming cells (GM‐CFC) in 17 of 27 patients and burst‐forming unit (BFU) erythroid in 12 of 27 patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the in vitro effects of recombinant TNF binding protein (rTBP1) on hematopoiesis of patients infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
the role of the soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) in the pathogenesis of hematopoietis in HIV infected individuals.
the effects of recombinant tumor necrosis factor‐binding protein (rTBP) in vitro on the hematopoiesis of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the in vitro effects of recombinant TNF binding protein on hematopoiesis of human immunodeficiency virus‐infected patients is that the recombinant TNFBP‐1 (TBP‐1), which is a soluble form of p55 TNF receptor (sTNFR), can enhance the growth of hematopoiesis in HIV‐infecetd patients.
TBP‐1 may be a promising agent in the treatment of HIV‐infected individuals who are not responding to HAART.
the in vitro effects of recombinant TBP‐1 in HIV‐infed patients with hematopoietic deficiency is promising.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rTBP‐I, a soluble TNF receptor, was able to induce dose‐dependent increase of GM‐CFC and BFU‐E from AIDS patients, but not from normal subjects.

rTBP‐I, in the concentrations used, does not affect the hematopoietis of HIV‐infected individuals who were treated with HAART, but does have the ability to enhance the hematopoiesis of patients with AIDS.
the TNF‐α antagonist, rTBP-1, can enhance hematopoietic colony formation in patients with HIV infection and AIDS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of TBP‐1 as a therapeutic agent for hematopoietic recovery in HIV‐inflicted patients should be evaluated in clinical trials.
TNF‐α is a key player in hematopoietic deficiency of patients with AIDS and that TNF‐alpha antagonist may be used as a treatment option for patients with HIV infection.
the use of TNF‐α binding protein (TBP) in patients with HIV infection can improve the number of hematopoietically active stem cells.
